clue.text: Fruit in season reportedly

indicators.note: What is reported is passed on by word of mouth, so what the clue wants is the sound of a word and not its spelling.

parts.note: produce that is in season is current, and the ear cannot tell the two spellings apart

explanation.surface: Fruit that the greengrocer says is at the right time of year for it.
explanation.walkthrough: Two spellings, one sound, and only the grid decides which is wanted. Currants are named after Corinth, whose dried grapes were shipped as raisins of Corauntz.
explanation.definitionFit: A currant is the small berry of the blackcurrant or redcurrant bush, sold and eaten as fruit.

clue.text: Hidden store of money received by auditors

indicators.note: Auditors take in what is put to them by ear, so the word reaches them as a sound rather than as a spelling.

parts.note: money is cash, and the two words are said exactly alike

explanation.surface: A secret fund that the accountants somehow got their hands on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Auditors' carries the accountant and the listener at once, both of them from Latin audire, to hear. A cache is a store put out of sight deliberately, not one merely mislaid.
explanation.definitionFit: A cache is a supply hidden on purpose and meant to be come back for, whether of food, weapons or money.

clue.text: All-day game of golf with a particular grandfather?

parts.note: a game of golf is a round
a grandfather is a tall longcase clock, so the particular grandfather meant is the clock

explanation.surface: A full day of golf played in the company of one particular grandfather.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks a definition by example run backwards: grandfather is one sort of clock, and you are asked to climb from the example to the class it sits in.
explanation.definitionFit: Something round the clock carries on through every hour there is, which is what an all-day affair does.

clue.text: More quickly beheaded flower

indicators.note: To behead a word is to take off the letter it starts with, the head being the front and never the tail.

parts.note: more quickly is FASTER, which gives up the F at its head

explanation.surface: A flower that lost its head in a hurry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' is the standing trap in these puzzles, where it often means a thing that flows, a river; here it is an honest plant. Asters are the daisy-shaped michaelmas blooms of late summer.
explanation.definitionFit: An aster is a garden perennial with rayed, daisy-like blooms, so the plain word flower covers it.

clue.text: One out of the bowls tour, even losing round and down by five

indicators.note: A word losing something has it taken away, so the letter named next goes missing from what stands in front.
To be down by an amount is to be short of exactly that much, so the letter it names is missing from the word before.

parts.note: TOUR arrives one letter short, and the next block says which letter
a round is drawn as an O — the letter the tour gives up
EVEN comes in a letter short in the same way
five in Roman numerals is V, the letter taken out of EVEN

explanation.surface: A bowls player out of the tour, beaten in a round and trailing by five shots.
explanation.walkthrough: Bowls is the British lawn game played on a flat green, and a tour of it is a season of tournaments, which is what lets 'round' and 'five' dress up as scoring. A tureen is the lidded bowl soup arrives at table in.
explanation.definitionFit: A tureen is the deep covered bowl soup is served from, so it belongs to the class of bowls the clue points at.

clue.text: Fleshy fruit initially preserved

parts.note: the fruit left unnamed is the plum

indicators.note: 'Initially' asks how a word stands at its start, which is the single letter it opens with.

parts.note: the letter the word begins with

explanation.surface: Ripe fruit that was bottled at the very start of the season.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fruit' is deliberately vague and the plum is the one wanted, as it usually is in a short gap. Of fruit, plump means rounded and full of juice rather than overweight.
explanation.definitionFit: Something plump is filled out and soft under the hand, which is what fleshy says of a body or a ripe fruit.

clue.text: Start up again after parking for dare

indicators.note: What comes after a thing is written below it in a down entry, so the parking letter goes down first and the rest follows it.

parts.note: P is the letter on a parking sign
to start up again is to resume

explanation.surface: Firing the engine back up once the car has been parked, on a dare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dare' is the sense that survives in 'I would not presume': to presume to do a thing is to take the liberty of doing it without being asked.
explanation.definitionFit: To presume to do something is to venture it without leave, which is what dare means when an infinitive follows it.

clue.text: The responsibility of those who are very little with it

parts.note: if a job is up to you, it is your responsibility
minute means very small, and 'the' in front of an adjective names the people it describes

explanation.surface: A duty that falls on the very smallest people, who carry it about with them.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer ends on minute the adjective, said mi-NEWT and meaning tiny, which is the same six letters as the sixty seconds. 'With it' has been slang for abreast of the fashion since the 1960s.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone with it is keeping pace with what is current, and up to the minute says the same of news or style that has not aged a second.

clue.text: What could be threatening number in harbour

indicators.note: One thing in another is written inside it, so the number is set within the harbour.

parts.note: a harbour is a port, and the word parts after three letters
the number left unnamed is ten

explanation.surface: Something menacing counted among the ships tied up in the harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole opening phrase and not just its last word, which is why nothing in it can be a noun on its own. Portentous has drifted from the same root to mean merely pompous.
explanation.definitionFit: A portent is an advance sign of what is coming, and the word is nearly always kept for warnings of something bad.

clue.text: Tenerife court reformed forger

indicators.note: Something reformed has been formed again in another shape, so the letters in front are built back up in a new order.

parts.note: the thirteen letters of TENERIFE COURT rearranged

explanation.surface: A court in Tenerife that turned a forger into an honest man.
explanation.walkthrough: A place name and a noun read as one thing, so nobody counts them, which is the whole cover for thirteen letters of fodder. Tenerife is the largest of Spain's Canary Islands, off the coast of Morocco.
explanation.definitionFit: A counterfeiter makes false money or goods and passes them as real, which is the forger's trade.

clue.text: Publicly approve of some bits of Southend or Seaford

indicators.note: Some bits of a thing are a part of it and not the whole, so a run of letters is lifted out of the words that follow.

parts.note: the run straddling all three words: southENDORSEaford

explanation.surface: Coming out in favour of certain parts of two English seaside towns.
explanation.walkthrough: Southend-on-Sea in Essex and Seaford in Sussex are both English resorts, which is what makes the pairing read as a genuine opinion. The join runs straight through the 'or', where nobody thinks to look.
explanation.definitionFit: To endorse something is to declare yourself behind it in public; the original sense is a signature written on the back of a document.

clue.text: Loose relative giving up first

indicators.note: A word giving up its first hands over the letter it begins with and keeps the rest.

parts.note: the relative is an AUNTIE, parting with the A she starts with

explanation.surface: A relative of loose habits who was the first to give in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loose' is the verb rather than the adjective the surface offers: to loose a knot is to untie it. Auntie and not aunt is the relative wanted, the pet form being ordinary enough in Britain to pass as the plain word.
explanation.definitionFit: To loose something is to slacken or free it, and untying is how a rope, a knot or a boat gets loosed.

clue.text: Ball with son and papa present

parts.note: S is son, as written on a family tree
P is papa in the radio alphabet
someone present is here

explanation.surface: A dance at which the son and the father both turned up.
explanation.walkthrough: Papa is the radio alphabet's P and not another word for father, a trap the son sets up two words earlier by behaving itself. The ball wanted is the geometer's, not the dancing one.
explanation.definitionFit: A sphere is a perfectly round solid, the shape every ball is made to be.

clue.text: Small amount of broth, cold, available from the menu

parts.note: broth is a thin soup
C is cold, as marked on a tap
a dish the kitchen can still serve is on

explanation.surface: A chilled broth among the things the kitchen can still manage tonight.
explanation.walkthrough: Soupçon is French for suspicion, taken into English for the barest trace of a flavour, and written there with a cedilla the grid cannot hold. The soup at its front is coincidence the setter has made the most of.
explanation.definitionFit: A soupçon is the merest dash of something — a small amount of a flavour, or of any quality at all.

clue.text: Looking embarrassed about bad tear in tyre

indicators.note: What is written about a subject goes all the way round it, so the first word opens up and the rest is set inside.
A bad thing has gone wrong, and letters that have gone wrong are no longer standing in their proper order.

parts.note: anyone embarrassed goes red in the face, and the word opens after two letters
the four letters of TEAR put in another order

explanation.surface: A blush over a nasty rip in the tyre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tear' is the rip that rhymes with bare, though the eye offers the weeping one first; either way it is four letters to shuffle. A retread is a worn casing given a fresh layer of rubber and sold round again.
explanation.definitionFit: A retread is a tyre whose worn tread has been replaced with new rubber, and it is sold and fitted as a tyre in its own right.

clue.text: Stand-in ruler, for instance during split

indicators.note: What happens during something happens inside it, so the shorter piece is written within the longer.

parts.note: a split in cloth or rock is a rent, and the word parts after its first letter
e.g. is the everyday shortening of the Latin for 'for instance'

explanation.surface: A caretaker monarch installed while the country was coming apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For instance' looks like the setter softening the definition, which is what those two words normally do, when here they are two letters of the answer. Britain's Regency was George IV's, ruling in place of his father during the king's madness.
explanation.definitionFit: A regent holds a throne's power for a monarch who is absent, ill or too young, without ever being the monarch.

clue.text: Partially glance towards window

indicators.note: Something done partially is done in part only, so part of what follows is taken and not the whole of it.

parts.note: the run sitting across the two words: gLANCE Towards

explanation.surface: Half an eye cast in the direction of the window.
explanation.walkthrough: A lancet is the tall narrow pointed window of early Gothic churches, named for the surgeon's blade whose shape it copies. The Lancet, Britain's medical journal, was named from the same instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: A lancet is a slim window with a sharply pointed arch, the standard form in early English church building.

clue.text: Complete reduction in funding by United Nations

indicators.note: Read as 'done by', the word names the doer, and the doer is written in front of the deed.

parts.note: the United Nations is known by its two initials
a reduction in funding is a cut

explanation.surface: The United Nations slashing what it pays out.
explanation.walkthrough: Complete is the film-cataloguer's sense: an uncut print is the whole of it with nothing trimmed. Taking 'by' as 'done by' rather than 'beside' is what settles which piece goes first.
explanation.definitionFit: An uncut version has had nothing taken out of it, so it stands complete as it was first made.

clue.text: Brought into operation, program gave false answers

parts.note: a program on a phone is an app
to give false answers is to lie

explanation.surface: A piece of software caught coming out with untruths.
explanation.walkthrough: Applied is the past tense here — applied the brakes, applied a rule — and not the adjective of 'applied mathematics'. App is the newest of the crossword shortenings and still earns its keep three letters at a time.
explanation.definitionFit: To apply something is to put it to work on a job, so whatever has been applied has been brought into operation.

clue.text: Jacket father used around ship

indicators.note: What is used around a thing is wrapped about it, so the father's two letters part and go outside.

parts.note: pa is father, and the two letters open to take the ship in
the ship left unnamed is the Ark

explanation.surface: The coat father wore aboard the ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ship' unspecified in a three-letter space is almost always Noah's, the one vessel everybody can name. Parka came into English from Nenets by way of Russian, and means a hooded skin coat.
explanation.definitionFit: A parka is a long hooded coat made for hard winters, which is a jacket of the heaviest kind.

clue.text: What begins day — it's the tiny yellowhammer's simple song

indicators.note: What begins a word is the letter it starts with, and each word in the run that follows gives one.

parts.note: the opening letters of those five words, taken in order

explanation.surface: The little yellowhammer's song that gets the morning started.
explanation.walkthrough: The yellowhammer is a British farmland bunting whose song is a short repeated phrase, heard by country tradition as 'a little bit of bread and no cheese'. The dash is punctuation and counts for nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: A ditty is a short, light song with nothing elaborate about it, which is what a simple song is.

clue.text: Type of TV system terminated by revolution

parts.note: a business terminated is closed
one revolution of a wheel is one circuit of its track

explanation.surface: A television network shut down by the men who seized the palace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolution' hands over its dullest sense, a single turn, while the surface keeps the barricades. Closed-circuit pictures travel only along their own wiring to the monitors on the end of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Closed-circuit television sends its pictures down its own cabling to fixed monitors instead of broadcasting them, so it is one type of TV system.

clue.text: Defenceless, attacked with nuclear weapons when uranium is key

indicators.note: Uranium is U on the periodic table and a key in music is A, and saying the one is the other stands the A where the U had been.

parts.note: to nuke a place is to attack it with nuclear weapons — five letters, one of them about to be traded

explanation.surface: A country with nothing left to defend itself, bombed because its uranium was what mattered.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole surface is built to make 'key' mean crucial, and it is the musical one, A. Naked keeps the exposed sense in phrases like the naked eye and naked aggression.
explanation.definitionFit: Naked means stripped of covering, and whatever has lost its cover has nothing left between it and an attacker.

clue.text: Stonework destroyed car tyre

indicators.note: What is destroyed has been broken up, and letters broken up have to be put back together in some other order.

parts.note: the seven letters of CAR TYRE rearranged

explanation.surface: Masonry lying in the road that wrecked a car tyre.
explanation.walkthrough: Tracery is the branching stone ribwork that holds the glass in a Gothic window, so calling it stonework is exact rather than loose. Masons classed it as plate or bar tracery depending on whether the stone was pierced or moulded.
explanation.definitionFit: Tracery is carved openwork stone, most often the ribs dividing the lights of a church window.
